judge.reasoning:
Tool/metric selection is strong and well-matched to the business: the agent correctly prioritized (1) share of young children under 10, (2) Hispanic population share plus limited-English-proficiency households — both essential for a bilingual immersion daycare — followed by income/education for tuition affordability, labor force participation as a proxy for childcare demand, and home ownership as a stability/retention signal. The importance weighting (92→55) is sensible and each section is justified against the brief. This earns high section_relevance and tool_selection_relevance.

However, the analysis has a critical granularity mismatch that hurts overall usefulness. The brief explicitly asks for 'family-dense neighborhoods... near residential subdivisions and employer corridors,' i.e., ZIP or neighborhood-level site selection. The report claims zip_count=10 but actually reports at the COUNTY level (Harris, Fort Bend, Montgomery, etc.). Counties like Harris (4.85M people) are far too coarse for choosing a specific lease site; the owner cannot pick a $6–9K lease location from a county map. This is the main reason overall_quality is only mediocre despite good metric choices.

Data plausibility is mostly good: Houston metro ~7.4M, median income ~$89K, Fort Bend as the high-income/high-education county, and Harris leading Hispanic share (~43%) all ring true. Minor concerns: the summary median_household_income of $89K sits at the very top of the stated $69–89K range rather than the middle, and the narrative cites 'college attainment 9.5%–36.3%' while the chart only shows the high end (24–36%), so the low bound isn't substantiated by shown data.

Visualization appropriateness is the weakest area. The Family Age Structure chart is titled 'Share of Young Children Under 10 Across Counties' and subtitled as a county ranking, but the categorical_data is actually an age-bracket breakdown (Under 10, 10–19, 20s, 30s, 40s) — a title/data mismatch. A distribution or a proper county-ranking bar was intended but the data doesn't match either the title or the stated purpose. The bubble chart (Hispanic % vs LEP %, sized by population) is a genuinely appropriate multi-dimensional choice and is the strongest visual. Remaining bars are appropriate for categorical county comparisons but are truncated to 5 rows despite claiming top-10.

Narrative is specific and ties to real figures, avoids pure filler, and offers actionable ideas (tiered pricing, workshops as lead-gen). It loses points for the county-vs-neighborhood mismatch and for citing ranges (e.g., 9.5% education, 11.1% under-10 low end) not visible in the shown data.
